digests.standfirst: The body that certifies what governments are allowed to call the best available science spent a week in Addis Ababa and decided neither when its next assessment arrives nor how next year is paid for; its chair suspended the session rather than put it to a room the poorest delegations had already left. In the same week a Himalayan research centre published a reconstruction of August's cross-border disaster showing the slope had been moving measurably for forty-eight days before it failed — which is close to the opposite of the conclusion an attribution study drew a month earlier about what could have been foreseen, and which lands six days before a climate fund's board meets in emergency session, for the first time in its existence, to consider paying for it.

The strongest El Niño yet measured is being managed, for now, by the institutions that forecast it rather than by the ones that would have to respond: a famine early-warning system put the whole 2026–27 event on the record in one global report, and the Horn of Africa's famine risk changed its driver from drought to flood without changing magnitude. In the same week the presidency of November's climate conference answered a finance shortfall by reaching into the defence budget — "what does it mean to spend 5% for defense if you don't have a country to live on?" — while a draft of the European Union's own negotiating position said there is no scope for new climate finance at all.

Three of this week's developments were not about a hazard but about the instruments the field measures hazards with. Two United Nations agencies told governments that the radio spectrum weather satellites physically depend on is being competed away; Fiji went into the pre-conference talks defending the climate panel's standing as the reference science against states that would prefer another body; and the only price yet put on Europe's lethal summer came from a credit insurer's proprietary model rather than from any journal. Against that, the sole standing United Nations machinery for climate and security turns out to have received $18.27 million in nine years, and in Nepal a flood warning that reached close to a million telephones was followed by forty-three deaths, almost all of them in landslides.

For the first time the whole United Nations membership has agreed that a state does not stop being a state when its territory goes under water, and that its ocean boundaries hold where its coastline does not — and the United States did not block it. In the same week NATO published the first revision of its resilience baseline in a decade, with extreme weather written in and the words climate change written out, while a British foreign secretary told the security community that climate belongs in threat assessments and then routed £1 million of a £331 million package to the only standing multilateral machinery the field has. Somalia's government and the United Nations asked for money to act on a flood forecast that is about as close to certain as forecasts get, and did not get it.

The attribution scientists who spent three weeks declining to say whether warming caused the Himalayan disaster published on 17 September and did something neither side of that argument expected: they refused the event-level question, attributed the conditions that produced it, and declared the event past the limits of what adaptation could have prevented. Within twenty-four hours Nepal's finance minister was in New Delhi using the finding. Meanwhile the Dutch budget answered a request to double water spending by funding the one thing the request said was already funded, and the United States finalised the repeal of its power-plant carbon rules on the floor of a G20 energy meeting whose only outcome document does not contain the word climate.

The UN's climate secretariat takes the security frame to the European Parliament and calls the summer a continent-wide economic security emergency; the Netherlands' delta commissioner asks the cabinet to double water spending to two per cent of GDP and says plainly that not all damage can now be prevented; and Nepal puts a $4.78 billion reconstruction bill to the world in the same week its scientists agree publicly that they cannot attribute the disaster that caused it.

The UN Environment Programme concedes that 1.5°C will be crossed and asks governments to manage the overshoot instead; small island states and Pacific leaders refuse the frame within forty-eight hours; and a Himalayan disaster turns into an argument about which monitoring system should have caught it.

Two multilateral instruments fail in one week, the military climate-security reporting infrastructure is found to have quietly stopped publishing, and attribution claims run wrong in both directions on two different disasters.
